chapters.1: John introduces this book as a revelation of Jesus Christ given to show God's servants what must soon happen, written while John was exiled on the island of Patmos. He describes a stunning vision of the risen Christ, glorious and powerful, standing among seven golden lampstands and holding seven stars, who tells John not to be afraid and instructs him to write what he sees and send it to seven churches.
chapters.2: Christ dictates personal messages to the churches in Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira, praising each for specific strengths like perseverance or faithfulness under persecution, while correcting specific failures such as losing their first love, tolerating false teaching, or sexual immorality. Each message ends with a promise to those who "overcome."
chapters.3: Christ continues with messages to the churches in Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. Sardis looks alive but is spiritually dead, Philadelphia is commended for faithfulness despite limited strength, and Laodicea is rebuked for being lukewarm and self-satisfied, with Christ urging them to repent and reopen the door to him.
chapters.4: John is taken up in a vision to heaven, where he sees God seated on a throne surrounded by rainbow-like light, twenty-four elders, and four unusual living creatures covered in eyes. The creatures and elders continuously worship God, declaring his holiness and his role as creator of all things.
chapters.5: John sees a sealed scroll that no one is found worthy to open, until a Lamb who appears to have been slain, but is standing, takes the scroll, honored as both the Lion of Judah and the sacrificial Lamb. Heaven erupts in worship, with every creature declaring the Lamb worthy to receive power, honor, and glory.
chapters.6: The Lamb opens the first six of seven seals on the scroll, releasing four horsemen representing conquest, war, famine, and death, along with the cries of martyred souls under the altar and a great cosmic upheaval when the sixth seal opens. The chapter ends with terrified people hiding and asking who can possibly survive God's judgment.
chapters.7: Before continuing the judgments, an angel marks 144,000 servants of God, listed by Israel's twelve tribes, to protect them from the coming harm. John then sees a vast, uncountable multitude from every nation standing before God's throne in white robes, identified as those who have come through great tribulation and are now comforted and cared for by God.
chapters.8: The seventh seal is opened, leading to seven angels with seven trumpets. As the first four trumpets sound, plagues strike a third of the earth, sea, rivers, and sky, bringing destruction described in dramatic, symbolic terms, with a warning that worse woes are still to come.
chapters.9: The fifth trumpet unleashes a swarm of locust-like creatures from the abyss that torment, but don't kill, people without God's seal, for five months. The sixth trumpet releases an army of 200 million that kills a third of humanity, yet the survivors still refuse to turn from their idols and wrongdoing.
chapters.10: A mighty angel appears holding a small scroll and declares with a solemn oath that there will be no more delay before God's plan reaches its completion. John is told to eat the scroll, which tastes sweet in his mouth but turns bitter in his stomach, and he's told he must prophesy again to many nations.
chapters.11: John measures the temple and learns of two witnesses who will prophesy for a set time, be killed by the beast, then be miraculously raised and taken up to heaven, which terrifies onlookers. The seventh trumpet then sounds, announcing that God's kingdom has triumphantly come, prompting worship in heaven and revealing God's temple with the ark inside it.
chapters.12: John sees a vision of a woman clothed in heavenly glory about to give birth, threatened by a great red dragon that tries to devour her child, but the child is caught up to God's throne. A war breaks out in heaven where the dragon, identified as Satan, is defeated and thrown down to earth, where he continues to pursue the woman and her offspring.
chapters.13: A terrifying beast rises from the sea, given authority and worship by the dragon, and makes war on God's people for a set period of time. A second beast then arises from the earth, performing deceptive miracles to force everyone to worship the first beast and receive its mark, introducing the mysterious number 666.
chapters.14: John sees the Lamb with the 144,000 standing victorious on Mount Zion, followed by angels announcing the gospel, Babylon's coming fall, and warnings against worshipping the beast. The chapter closes with a dramatic harvest image, where the earth is reaped and a great harvest of grapes is trodden in God's winepress of judgment.
chapters.15: John sees a sign in heaven of seven angels prepared with the seven final plagues, while those who had resisted the beast stand victorious, singing a song of praise to God's justice and holiness. The heavenly temple opens, and the seven angels receive golden bowls filled with God's wrath, with the temple so full of God's glory that no one can enter it until the plagues are finished.
chapters.16: The seven angels pour out their bowls of judgment one by one, bringing sores, turning waters to blood, scorching heat, darkness, and a massive earthquake that reshapes the world. These climactic plagues lead to the gathering of earthly powers for a final battle at a place called Armageddon.
chapters.17: John sees a vision of a woman called "Babylon," dressed in luxury and riding a scarlet beast, representing a corrupt system allied with worldly power that has persecuted God's people. An angel explains the symbolism of the beast and its heads and horns, and describes how these allied powers will eventually turn on the woman and destroy her themselves.
chapters.18: A powerful angel announces the sudden fall of "Babylon the great," a city whose excess and corruption had enriched and corrupted the nations and their rulers. Kings, merchants, and sailors who profited from her mourn her sudden destruction, while heaven is called to rejoice because God has judged her for her crimes.
chapters.19: Heaven erupts in celebration over Babylon's fall and anticipates the wedding celebration between the Lamb and his bride. John then sees a vision of Christ returning as a victorious rider on a white horse, defeating the beast and the false prophet, who are thrown into a lake of fire, while their armies are destroyed.
chapters.20: Satan is bound for a thousand years while those who remained faithful reign with Christ, a period often called the millennium, after which Satan is released briefly before being finally defeated. The chapter ends with a vision of a final judgment before a great white throne, where everyone is judged according to their deeds, and death itself is thrown into the lake of fire.
chapters.21: John sees a new heaven and new earth, along with the holy city, New Jerusalem, descending from God, where there is no more death, sorrow, or pain, since God himself lives among his people. He describes the city's dazzling beauty and precious materials in extensive detail, emphasizing that God's own presence replaces any need for a temple.
chapters.22: John describes the river of life and the tree of life in the new creation, where God's servants will see his face and reign with him forever without night or curse. The book closes with a series of urgent promises and warnings about Christ's soon return, instructions to keep the words of this prophecy unaltered, and an invitation for anyone thirsty to freely come and drink the water of life.
